extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers interested in public opinion, political communication, and political history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles about how public opinion is formed and how political language, symbols, timing, and authority shape mass attitudes. Emphasis on rhetorical techniques (vagueness, symbolism), audience differences, and strategic message construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heal schisms by selecting non-explosive subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker must heal schisms by skilfully selecting opening subjects that ignore past schisms and avoid explosive conflicts (e.g., choosing the spoils system in diplomatic appointments to bridge divided Republicans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an introduction that evokes shared history and a common mood; avoid reminding audiences of the original schism or of issues that would reopen intense factional conflict. Example: Hughes used a non-contentious topic to re-unite Republicans divided since 1912.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vagueness/symbolic ambiguity to unify factions
rubrics_metrics.description: Let words and formulas mean different things to different factions so that a single phrase can cover opposing purposes (e.g., 'American rights' meant coercion to pro-Allies and protection against British sea power to pro-Germans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ deliberately elastic phrases or symbolic formulas to repress sharp issue-divisions and create superficial harmony; be aware this sacrifices intellectual clarity for broader emotional coalition. Example: stretching the word 'intervention' to include varied meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress irreconcilable issues when building coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are questions on which groups cannot agree, political actors may obliterate or avoid them to gain support from mutually incompatible factions (e.g., pretending the Lusitania question does not exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not press matters that are unresolvable within the target coalition; omission can be a deliberate rhetorical tactic to maintain unity, though it may obscure reality and leave a policy vacuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional conditioning and symbolic substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions aroused by concrete events fade and are replaced by substitute pictures, names, or symbols; conditioned responses mean many different stimuli can arouse the same emotion and many different responses can satisfy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that public feeling often operates through second-hand images and names rather than direct facts; deliberately link desired emotions to durable symbols or personifications (e.g., feed the emotion by associating it with a symbol like 'Mr. Hoover' or 'Americanism').

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols must be introduced by authoritative people at opportune moments
rubrics_metrics.description: A symbol acquires power only when spoken by people who are strategically placed and at the right moment; otherwise the words are mere wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan not only the symbol but its bearer and timing (the 'earmarking'); effectiveness depends on the introducer's perceived authority and the situational receptivity of the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance specificity and universality in public statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Public policy statements intended to rally diverse audiences must be broad enough to include many factions yet concrete enough to be plausible as possible peace terms or aims (as with the Fourteen Points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design clauses to meet national aspirations without provoking official disunion; use structure (e.g., numbering) and carefully chosen words to convey business-like precision while retaining flexibility to cover multiple contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical form and phrasing strategically (numbering, precise word choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical devices—such as numbering, precise dates/words, and careful choice of verbs—are used to create impressions of precision, to signal intended boundaries, and to manipulate interpretation (e.g., preferring 'righted' and '1871' rather than 'restored').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick wording that can satisfy different expectations simultaneously and use form (numbering, lists) to convey seriousness and manage interpretations across audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of over-simplification and verbalism
rubrics_metrics.description: As people substitute names and shorthand for full situations, they risk lapsing into verbalism—talking about names regardless of objects and losing the link between words and reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against forgetting that names are substitutes; keep track of what has been simplified to avoid misalliances or false equivalences between ideas and the objects they once named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and lifecycle of symbols (bursting of symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols can 'burst' if abused or if reality resists their uses; too violent an abuse or excessive resistance in the symbol's name will destroy its unifying power (e.g., Holy Russia's symbol burst under suffering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor whether a symbol continues to map onto constituents' experiences; avoid overextending or rigidly defending a symbol when its underlying conditions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol vs omnibus: grounding in lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A true symbol is rooted in broad, shared experience and can endure; an 'omnibus' (abstract idea) that lacks experiential grounding tends to create only transient harmonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer symbols that connect to genuine experiences and memories of the audience rather than abstract, omnibus labels if the goal is durable integration; recognize that scope of symbol may increase or shrink over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use antithetical/common enemy symbols to unite disparate groups
rubrics_metrics.description: To amalgamate conflicting factions, find a symbol that stands as the antithesis of what they all hate (e.g., 'Americanism' read differently by isolationists, Wilson-haters, and anti-revolutionaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select symbols that can be read in diverse, compatible ways by different groups—each group interprets the symbol according to its own grievances—thus producing a coalition without detailed program agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience heterogeneity: differing susceptibility to distant ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: People vary widely in how vividly they respond to distant or abstract stimuli; some are aroused by far-off images (e.g., starving child in Russia) as strongly as by immediate sight, others are nearly insensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment messaging and symbols with awareness of audience differences; some appeals will mobilize emotionally remote constituencies while others will require closer, experiential triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority selection: trust as the bridge to unknown matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Where facts are out of sight, people choose among reporters and authorities based on trustability; the introducer of a symbol often becomes the perceived authority associated with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate or identify trusted intermediaries (parents, teachers, prominent public figures, newspapers) to introduce and legitimize symbols and messages; credibility of the source is often more decisive than the truth of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurantism results from aiming for superficial harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: When superficial harmony is the aim while conflict is the fact, public appeals tend toward obscurantism—vagueness at crucial points is a symptom of cross-purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that deliberate vagueness to avoid conflict produces an obscuring of real differences; this may achieve temporary coalition but at the cost of clarity and later conflict when specifics are required.
